title: Threads and the Scheduler
summary: A **thread** is a path of execution with its own registers and its own stack, running inside a process and sharing everything else. The **scheduler** decides which threads run on which cores and for how long. This lesson creates threads with `std::thread` and the Windows API, splits work between them, and explains what the scheduler does with them.
markdown:
## What a thread has of its own All threads of a process share its address space, its heap, its globals and its handles. Each thread has only a few things of its own: | Per thread | Why | |---|---| | Registers, including `rip` and `rsp` | So it can be paused and resumed exactly where it was | | A stack (1 MB reserved by default) | For its own calls and locals (lessons 1.05, 2.01) | | Thread-local storage | Variables declared `thread_local` | | A thread id, a priority, a last-error value | `GetLastError` is per thread | Because memory is shared, threads can work on the same data with no copying. That is their great advantage and, as the next lesson shows, their great danger. ## Creating threads The portable way is `std::thread` (or `std::jthread` in C++20, which joins itself automatically): ```cpp #include #include #include #include int main() { std::vector values(10'000'000); std::iota(values.begin(), values.end(), 1); // 1, 2, 3, ... 10,000,000 const unsigned parts{ 4 }; std::vector partial(parts, 0); // one result slot per thread: no sharing std::vector workers; const std::size_t chunk{ values.size() / parts }; for (unsigned t{ 0 }; t < parts; ++t) { const std::size_t begin{ t * chunk }; const std::size_t end{ t == parts - 1 ? values.size() : begin + chunk }; workers.emplace_back([&values, &partial, t, begin, end] { long long sum{ 0 }; for (std::size_t i{ begin }; i < end; ++i) sum += values[i]; partial[t] = sum; }); } for (std::thread& w : workers) w.join(); // wait for every thread to finish std::cout << "total " << std::accumulate(partial.begin(), partial.end(), 0LL) << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` total 50000005000000 ``` The pattern is the simplest safe one: each thread works on its own slice and writes its own result slot; the main thread waits with `join` and combines the results. Nothing is written by two threads, so nothing needs locking. A `std::thread` must be **joined** (waited for) or **detached** (left to run on its own) before it is destroyed; destroying a joinable thread calls `std::terminate`. `std::jthread` joins in its destructor, which is why it is usually the better choice. Underneath, on Windows, `std::thread` calls `CreateThread` (through the C runtime). The direct form: ```cpp DWORD WINAPI worker(void* parameter) { auto* job{ static_cast(parameter) }; job->run(); return 0; // the thread's exit code } HANDLE thread{ CreateThread(nullptr, 0, &worker, &job, 0, nullptr) }; WaitForSingleObject(thread, INFINITE); // like join() CloseHandle(thread); ``` The thread function is a callback (lesson 3.04) taking one `void*`, through which you pass whatever the thread needs. ## How many threads? `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` reports how many threads the processor can run truly at once: cores, doubled on processors with simultaneous multithreading (Hyper-Threading). Creating more threads than that for CPU-heavy work does not make it faster: the extra threads just take turns. Games usually create a fixed set of worker threads at start-up, about one per core minus one or two, and feed them small jobs through a queue (a **job system**). Creating a thread costs tens of microseconds and a megabyte of address space, far too much to do per task. ## The scheduler Windows decides, many times a second, which ready thread runs on each core: - Each thread has a **priority**. The highest-priority ready threads run first. - Threads of equal priority take turns in **time slices** (quanta) of a few milliseconds. - A thread that waits (for input, a file, a lock, `Sleep`) leaves the core straight away, and another thread runs. - Switching from one thread to another, a **context switch**, saves one thread's registers and loads another's. It costs a few microseconds. ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Ready
(wants a core)"] -->|"scheduler picks it"| X["Running"] X -->|"time slice used up, or a higher priority thread wakes"| R X -->|"waits: Sleep, a lock, I/O"| W["Waiting"] W -->|"the thing it waited for happens"| R ``` Things this explains in games: - `Sleep(1)` sleeps for **at least** a millisecond, often up to 15.6 ms with the default timer resolution. A frame limiter built on `Sleep` is imprecise (chapter 10). - A game whose main thread spins in a busy loop takes a core at 100% for nothing. - Raising a thread's priority rarely helps and can starve other threads, including Windows' own; leave priorities alone unless you have measured a reason. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Destroying a `std::thread` without joining it > The program terminates. Join it, detach it, or use `std::jthread`. > [!warning] Capturing locals by reference in a thread that outlives them > The thread reads a dead stack frame. Join before the locals go out of scope, as the example does. > [!warning] One thread per task > Creating threads is expensive. Create a few workers once and give them jobs. > [!warning] Expecting `Sleep(1)` to sleep for exactly one millisecond > It sleeps for at least that, often much longer. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What does each thread have that is not shared with the other threads of its process? + Its registers and its stack - Its own heap - Its own copy of the global variables > Heap, globals, code and handles are shared; registers and stack are per thread. ? Why does the summing example give each thread its own slot in `partial`? + So no two threads write the same memory, and no locking is needed - Because threads cannot return values - To use less memory > Separate outputs, combined after `join`, is the simplest safe pattern. ? A thread calls `Sleep(5)`. What happens on its core? + The thread leaves the core, and the scheduler runs another ready thread - The core stays idle for 5 ms - The whole process pauses > A waiting thread gives up the core immediately. ? What does `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` tell you? + How many threads the processor can run truly in parallel - How many threads the process may create - How many threads are currently running > More CPU-bound threads than this only take turns. ```
ideas:
- Time the summing example with 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads in a Release build, using `std::chrono::steady_clock`.
- Pause it in Visual Studio while the workers run and open **Debug → Windows → Threads**. Double-click each worker to see its own call stack.
- Replace `std::thread` with `std::jthread` and remove the `join` loop.

cards.a: The scheduler saving one thread's registers and loading another's, so the core continues with a different thread.

cards.q: Why do games use a fixed set of worker threads instead of creating a thread per task?
cards.a: Creating a thread is slow and uses a stack's worth of address space; reusing a few workers fed from a job queue avoids that cost.

cards.q: What must happen to a `std::thread` before it is destroyed?
cards.a: It must be joined or detached, or the program terminates.
